extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers and Coursera learners interested in plot and fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: A short online course syllabus describing fundamentals of plotting for fictional prose: definitions and mechanics of plot, story structure, scene construction, showing vs telling, and revision practices including a 21-point revision checklist and peer-review assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot definitions and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: What is plot? How does plot shape a narrative? What makes a strong plot? How is plot different from a story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 1 introduces essentials about plot definitions and mechanics and examines how plot works in actual books (example: the Harry Potter series). The course frames plot as what keeps a story moving and manipulates feelings, expectations, and desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character + Action = Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Character + Action = Plot (explicit formula stated on the course page).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module content includes a video titled 'Character + Action = Plot' to show how choices characters make (actions) interact with character goals to create plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five key questions for creating a dynamic character
rubrics_metrics.description: The five key questions you should ask yourself when creating a dynamic character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 1 promises explicit questions to guide character creation; these feed into how character choices generate plot. (The page references the five questions but does not list them verbatim.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure: sequence events to maximize storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn what story structure is and how by understanding structure you can learn how to sequence the events in your plot to help maximize your own storytelling abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 2 covers sequencing events, using outlines and structure to organize stories you want to tell and to shape pacing and arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freytag's pyramid / five-act (ABDCE) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of Freytag's pyramid, the five act structure (ABDCE), and how that structure can be found in works of classic literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 2 includes examples from famous works and shows how to apply five-act/ABDCE structure in plotting scenes and the larger narrative arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes as the building blocks of storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes are the building blocks of storytelling: what is a scene? And how does a scene move plot forward?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 3 focuses on scene function and includes videos and examples explaining how individual scenes propel narrative momentum and connect to overall plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show vs Tell (showing and showing techniques)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between telling and showing (Show, Don't Tell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 3 includes a peer-review assignment titled 'Show, Don't Tell' and a video exploring techniques for making scenes sensory and active rather than expository.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five key elements each scene should have
rubrics_metrics.description: The five key elements each scene should have (stated as a module objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 3 promises explicit scene elements and provides examples of effective scenes; the page references a video on 'Examples of Effective Scenes' but does not list the five elements on the syllabus page itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and description to make a scene come alive
rubrics_metrics.description: How setting and description can make a scene come alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 3 includes discussion and examples showing how description and sensory detail contribute to scene vividness and reader immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and reversals
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative pacing and reversals as plot devices that keep the story moving and surprise the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course introduction states that pacing and reversals will be discussed as part of understanding plot mechanics and manipulating reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connecting beginning, middle, and end (narrative cohesion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connecting the beginning, middle and end (how plot ties together across a full narrative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course promises to reveal 'the inevitable surprise: connecting the beginning, middle and end,' teaching how scenes and structure should cohere into a unified arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and revision process
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifics of editing and revising your work: revision from first draft to subsequent drafts until manuscript is agent-ready.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 4 covers revision strategies, conversations with writers, and practical steps for editing toward submission; it emphasizes an iterative process from first to later drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: 21-point checklist for revising a completed first draft
rubrics_metrics.description: A twenty-one point checklist on what to do once you have a completed first draft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 4 includes a short video titled 'The 21st Point' describing a detailed checklist learners should apply during revision; the syllabus page references the checklist but does not enumerate the 21 items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creating characters with strong motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversations about creating characters with strong motivations (as part of revision and craft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 4 explicitly pairs revision work with ensuring characters have clear, strong motivations that drive actions and plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining language to rewrite vs language to cut
rubrics_metrics.description: How to define language that gets rewritten versus language that gets cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 4 discusses decision-making about prose: what to keep, what to rewrite, what to delete, helping writers streamline language during revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review assignments and feedback expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviews are part of modules (multiple peer-review assignments) with a 'Feedback Expectations for the Specialization' video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each module includes peer-review tasks (examples: 'The Escalator', 'What's Up, Doc?', 'Show, Don't Tell', 'Cut It Out', 'The Whole Story') with allotted completion times; the course provides guidance on feedback norms and expectations for peer assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of literary examples to illustrate techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Using examples from famous works (e.g., Harry Potter) to show plot and structure in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllabus highlights course videos that examine how plot functions in well-known books and classic literature to model techniques for learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical outlining and use of structure/outlines
rubrics_metrics.description: How structure and outlines can help organize the stories you want to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Module 2 emphasizes practical outlining methods tied to structural models (Freytag/ABDCE) to plan scenes and sequence events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment time expectations for peer review tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Each peer review task includes an expected time commitment (e.g., 120 minutes for some peer reviews, 60 minutes for others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course lists estimated completion times for peer-review assignments and modules so learners can plan substantive feedback and revision work.
